strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and timely problem: lightweight acceleration of diffusion sampling by optimizing solver coefficients and timestep schedules, rather than training full student models.

The proposed Generalized Solver parameterization is well-motivated: using a strong base solver (DPM-Solver++(3M)) as additive theoretical guidance with trained corrections, and adding weighted sums of all previous points, is a sensible generalization of LD3/S4S that empirically yields faster and more stable convergence (Table 3, Figure 3), with a controlled comparison ensuring equal trainable parameter counts.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive and unusually thorough for this subfield: 6 datasets spanning pixel-space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2), latent-space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256), and text-to-image (SD v1.5 on MS-COCO), across multiple NFE settings, against a wide range of training-free and training-based baselines.

The ablation studies are convincing: coefficient parameterization vs. S4S, adversarial loss contribution, GAN-weight insensitivity, dataset size requirements (1400-5000 samples), training time/memory/inference-time analyses, and cross-dataset generalization (Table 5).

The paper is transparent about limitations (backpropagation through the full solver, per-NFE training) and provides strong reproducibility support (pseudocode matching the implementation, full hyperparameter listings, public datasets and checkpoints, released code).

Consistently strong results: e.g., FID 4.05 vs. 6.35 (S4S Alt) on CIFAR10 at NFE=4, 7.86 vs. 10.63 on FFHQ at NFE=4, and clear improvements at very low NFE regimes where regression-based distillation is hardest.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The method is essentially a refinement of the existing LD3/S4S framework (solver/schedule parameter learning via distillation), combining known ideas: additive corrections to theoretically-derived coefficients, an extended linear multistep signature, and standard adversarial training (relativistic GAN / R3GAN) on top of a paired distillation loss. The conceptual step beyond S4S is modest.

The combination of distillation with adversarial loss is well-established in diffusion distillation (ADD, LADD, UMD, etc.); the novelty lies only in its application to the much smaller parameter space of sampler coefficients.

Some fairness concerns in the comparisons: (a) GAS's adversarial loss compares student outputs against teacher outputs while the pixel-space discriminator is pre-trained on the real dataset (e.g., FFHQ-64 discriminator used for both FFHQ and AFHQv2), which changes the effective objective relative to baselines without adversarial loss; (b) several S4S results are marked with daggers due to teacher FID mismatches, making some entries (e.g., S4S on LSUN, FID 20.89) difficult to interpret as a fair baseline.

The adversarial component gives mixed benefits: GAS does not uniformly improve over GS (e.g., ImageNet NFE=5-7, MS-COCO NFE=6-7, AFHQv2 NFE=10), and it increases training time 2-9x and requires larger training sets due to discriminator overfitting, so the cost-benefit of the second headline contribution is not fully established.

Scalability is limited: backpropagation through the entire multi-step solver inference restricts applicability to larger models/resolutions (acknowledged as a limitation), and a separate solver must be trained for each NFE setting, which weakens practical appeal relative to training-free solvers or model-level distillation.

The choice of 'one-plus' teacher (student NFE n distilled from teacher NFE n+1) in the SD experiments is a departure from the other experiments and reduces the apparent acceleration gain, yet the headline claim of 'superior performance under similar resource constraints' glosses over this regime difference.

No comparison against stronger one-step/few-step distillation families under compute-normalized settings beyond brief training-time discussion; the positioning against consistency-style methods is qualitative rather than empirical.

strengths: Broad empirical evaluation spanning pixel-space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2), latent-space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256), and text-to-image (Stable Diffusion on MS-COCO) settings, with comparisons against training-free solvers and multiple learned-solver baselines (LD3, S4S).

Thorough ablation studies: coefficient parameterization vs. S4S with matched trainable-parameter budget, adversarial loss contribution, adversarial loss weight sensitivity, dataset size requirements, training time, and memory usage.

Reasonable methodological framing: additive corrections to theoretically derived DPM-Solver++(3M) coefficients give a well-behaved initialization, and the distillation + relativistic adversarial loss (Table 4) usefully shows that lower regression loss does not always mean better FID.
Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), teacher generation protocols, and a stated code release.
Transparent discussion of limitations, including per-NFE retraining and backpropagation-through-inference scalability.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the parameterization is a natural generalization of LD3/S4S (freeing solver order and adding point terms), and combining distillation with a GAN loss is well established in diffusion distillation (ADD, SDXL-Turbo, UCD, etc.). The contribution is largely an engineering refinement of the S4S line of work.

Inconsistent head-to-head results undermine the central 'superior to existing methods' claim: on ImageNet-256, S4S Alt achieves better FID than GS at every NFE (e.g., 5.13 vs. 7.87 at NFE=4), and GAS only narrowly matches it; S4S also beats GS on MS-COCO at NFE=6-7. The footnote that some S4S numbers are the authors' own re-implementations (with a modified order constraint) raises fairness concerns about these comparisons.

No statistical significance or seed variance is reported for FID comparisons; many margin-of-victory numbers (e.g., 2.24 vs. 2.39, 4.32 vs. 4.30) are within typical FID noise, especially since FID is computed on different sample counts (50k vs. 30k for COCO) and the paper itself concedes FID unreliability at high NFE.

The 'preserving fine-grained details' motivation from the abstract is not directly validated with any perceptual or human evaluation; qualitative evidence (Figure 4, Appendix E) is anecdotal and cherry-picked ('selected' samples chosen by L1 distance between methods).

The adversarial component requires its own dataset size tuning (5000 vs. 1400), discriminator training from scratch in latent space, and 2-9 hours training per configuration; combined with separate training per NFE, practical applicability at scale (larger models, higher resolutions) remains unaddressed and only acknowledged as a limitation.

The method improves over an already trained model but cannot exceed the teacher; gains vanish as NFE grows (GAS sometimes slightly worse than GS, e.g., AFHQv2 NFE=10), narrowing the practical impact window to very low NFEs where regression-only distillation baselines like consistency-based methods also compete.

Presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is empty, Table 7b has formatting errors, and some claims (e.g., 'does not require additional training tricks') sit awkwardly next to the GAN training machinery with dataset-size and weight sensitivity requirements.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated method: the Generalized Solver parameterization (learned additive corrections on top of theoretically derived DPM-Solver++(3M) coefficients, plus a full-history linear multistep signature) is simple, easy to describe, and supported by a direct comparison with LD3 and S4S parameterizations (Table 1) that makes the contribution easy to follow.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 datasets (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2, LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256, Stable Diffusion/MS-COCO), spanning pixel-space, latent-space, and text-to-image settings, with substantial FID improvements in the low-NFE regime (e.g., 7.86 vs 10.63 on FFHQ at NFE=4).

Useful ablations: coefficient parameterization vs. S4S under matched parameter counts (Table 3, Fig. 3), adversarial loss effect on FID vs. distillation loss (Table 4, Fig. 4), dataset size, GAN-weight sensitivity (Fig. 6), cross-dataset transfer (Table 5), training time, memory, and inference time.

Good practical efficiency story: GS/GAS train in ~1-3 hours on a single GPU versus days for full distillation methods, with small training datasets (1400-5000 samples), no inference-time overhead, and detailed pseudocode (Algorithm 1) plus hyperparameter appendix aiding reproducibility.
Honest reporting of trade-offs, e.g., GAS sometimes increases distillation loss while improving FID, GAS can underperform GS at higher NFEs, and explicit discussion of scalability limitations.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the paper is largely a careful combination of existing ingredients — solver/schedule distillation from LD3/S4S, theoretical-coefficient guidance from DPM-Solver++, and adversarial loss from established GAN distillation practice (StyleGAN-T, ADD, etc.). The technical advancement is incremental even if effective.

Fairness of the headline comparison is questionable: baseline numbers (GITS, DMN, LD3, S4S) are largely taken from prior papers, trained under potentially different teacher solvers, schedules, and hardware (A100 vs. their H100), and S4S results on LSUN/MS-COCO are flagged as not directly comparable (dagger footnote). Ideally all baselines would be retrained under the identical teacher protocol.

Potential evaluation inflation from the adversarial component: for pixel-space experiments GAS uses pre-trained R3GAN discriminators trained on the same evaluation distributions (CIFAR10, FFHQ-64 used for FFHQ and AFHQv2). This data coupling makes the adversarial gains harder to interpret cleanly and could partly explain why a trained-from-scratch discriminator is used only in latent experiments.

Gains are concentrated in the very-low-NFE regime and are inconsistent elsewhere: at NFE>=5 the GAS improvement over GS is negligible or negative (e.g., ImageNet 4.87 vs 4.93; MS-COCO NFE=5-7), which weakens the claim of a uniformly superior method; the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this.

Stability and sensitivity of joint GAN-style training (discriminator trained jointly with solver parameters) is examined only via a single GAN-weight sweep on one dataset; more analysis of training instability across settings would strengthen the empirical claims.

The theoretical grounding for why adding weighted sums of all previous points helps is thin (framed only as 'over-parameterization may simplify training'); no analysis of when the learned corrections deviate meaningfully from the base solver.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six datasets (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2, LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet, MS-COCO/Stable Diffusion) covering pixel-space, latent-space, and text-to-image settings, with consistent FID improvements over strong baselines (GITS, DMN, LD3, S4S) especially in the low-NFE regime (e.g., 7.86 vs 10.63 on FFHQ NFE=4; 4.05 vs 6.35 on CIFAR10 NFE=4)

Well-motivated parameterization: additive corrections to theoretically derived DPM-Solver++(3M) coefficients plus inclusion of past points/velocities is a sensible inductive bias, and the ablations (Tables 5, 10, Figure 3) convincingly show faster, more stable training than S4S parameterizations under matched parameter counts and codebase

Careful treatment of the adversarial component: relativistic GAN loss with gradient penalties, ablation of loss choice and weight sensitivity, and explicit mode-collapse analysis via precision/recall/density/coverage showing improved coverage over GS

Thorough efficiency analysis: training time, memory usage, inference overhead, and training-set size requirements, all with concrete numbers; also checks generality via cross-dataset solver transfer (Table 7)
Strong reproducibility practices: pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters for all experiments, public datasets/checkpoints, and released code
weaknesses: Contribution is primarily incremental: the paradigm (gradient-based learning of solver coefficients and timestep schedules) follows LD3/S4S, and the adversarial augmentation is a well-established remedy from paired image-to-image translation and recent diffusion distillation (ADD, etc.); the novelty lies in engineering the parameterization rather than new principles

Fairness of comparisons is partially compromised: several key baseline entries are marked with dagger as using different teacher hyperparameters and 'cannot be fairly compared' (e.g., S4S Alt on LSUN and ImageNet reports FID worse than the raw DPM-Solver++ baseline, which is implausible), so the headline superiority over S4S in latent-space settings is not fully supported

Method fails at NFE=1-2 with very high FID (147-314 on FFHQ), limiting applicability precisely in the regime where acceleration matters most; also requires separate training per target NFE, which is acknowledged but unresolved

Backpropagation through the entire multi-step ODE rollout raises scalability concerns for larger/modern models (SDXL-scale, video); only SD v1.5 is tested at 512x512, and the limitations section concedes this is unaddressed
FID results appear to be single-run without variance reporting, and adversarial training inherently increases result variance; the diversity preservation is analyzed on only one dataset (ImageNet)

A minor tension exists between the abstract's claim of a method 'without additional training tricks' and the reality that GAS introduces a full GAN training pipeline (discriminator design, loss weights, gradient penalties, separate optimizers) with per-resolution configurations

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem—accelerating diffusion sampling under resource constraints—and the Generalized Solver parameterization (additive corrections to theoretically grounded DPM-Solver++(3M) coefficients, multistep signature using full point/velocity history) is reasonable and well-motivated
Evaluation breadth is good: 6 datasets spanning pixel space (CIFAR10, FFHQ, AFHQv2), latent space (LSUN-Bedroom, ImageNet-256), and text-to-image (SD v1.5 on MS-COCO), with multiple NFE regimes

The ablation studies are fairly thorough: theoretical guidance (Table 5), GAN loss choice (Table 6), comparison with S4S parameterizations under identical settings (Table 3, 10), GAN-weight sensitivity (Fig. 6), mode collapse analysis via precision/recall/coverage (Table 8), dataset size, training time, and memory measurements

Efficiency claims are quantitatively supported (training hours, inference wall-clock time, peak memory), and the reproducibility statement plus detailed appendix (pseudocode, hyperparameters) is a plus
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the paper is essentially an incremental combination of two known ideas—(i) solver coefficient/timestep optimization from LD3/S4S with an additive-parameterization twist, and (ii) adding a relativistic GAN loss to distillation, which is well established (ADD, SDXL-Turbo, etc.). The method contribution feels like engineering refinement rather than a new principle

Some headline comparisons are not apples-to-apples: for Stable Diffusion, the 'one-plus' teacher protocol (teacher NFE = student NFE + 1) is used for GAS, and baselines marked with dagger used teachers with 'significantly different hyperparameters', making Table 2c and parts of 2b hard to interpret fairly; the method also uses a pretrained R3GAN discriminator for pixel-space experiments while the discriminator is a substantial ingredient of the gains

GAS beats its own teacher on several settings (e.g., FID 4.05 vs teacher 2.03 at NFE=4 on CIFAR10 in Table 9, 3.98 vs 2.03 in Table 12b, and FID values on MS-COCO where GAS at NFE=4 is 14.71 vs teacher 14.10 with different NFE) — these irregularities, partly acknowledged by the authors themselves ('FID loses its correlation with perceived fidelity'), suggest the headline numbers warrant more caution and human evaluation is absent

The core contribution's gain over the strongest baseline (S4S Alt) is moderate in many cells and the advantage vanishes at higher NFE (e.g., ImageNet NFE>=6, where S4S Alt is comparable or better; MS-COCO gains are within noise), and GS alone frequently underperforms S4S Alt in low-NFE latent settings (e.g., ImageNet NFE=4: 7.87 vs 5.13)

Clear scalability limitations acknowledged by the authors: requires backprop through the entire sampling trajectory, per-NFE retraining, and the approach underperforms at NFE=1-2 (Appendix B.8, FIDs of 147/193 at NFE=1), which limits practical significance for the most compute-constrained regimes the paper motivates

The comparison with S4S relies on a reimplementation ('S4S does not provide an official implementation'), introducing potential implementation bias in the key baseline comparison; the official S4S paper's variant differences (Alt vs LMS vs LMS+PC) make the baseline selection somewhat opaque
Presentation is dense in Section 3.1, with the coefficient derivation (Eqs. 13-20) difficult to follow; clarity of the core formulation would benefit from a single clean statement of the final solver

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 diverse benchmarks (pixel-space CIFAR10/FFHQ/AFHQv2, latent-space LSUN/ImageNet, and text-to-image with Stable Diffusion) with consistent improvements over strong recent baselines (LD3, S4S, GITS, DMN, UniPC, iPNDM) at matched NFE.

The core idea of additive theoretical guidance (initializing/anchoring learned coefficients on DPM-Solver++(3M)) is well-motivated and clearly ablated (Table 5, Table 3, Table 10), demonstrating faster convergence and more stable training than the S4S parameterization under matched parameter counts and codebase.

The adversarial component is thoughtfully analyzed: relativistic GAN loss selection (Table 6), loss-weight insensitivity (Fig. 6), explicit mode-collapse check via precision/recall/density/coverage (Table 8), and an honest demonstration that distillation loss can anti-correlate with FID at low NFE (Table 4).

Extensive efficiency analysis: training time, memory usage, training dataset size (only 1400-5000 teacher samples needed), and no inference-time overhead, making the practical case for the method convincing.

Method is lightweight relative to diffusion distillation (hours vs. days), preserves generative properties better than CD (Table 9), and shows some cross-dataset transfer (Table 7). Thorough appendices with pseudocode and hyperparameters support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method is essentially (i) a broader parameterization of existing solver/timestep distillation (extending LD3/S4S) with a theoretical-solver initialization prior, and (ii) adding a standard adversarial loss to an existing regression distillation objective — both components individually draw on established ideas (Isola et al., R3GAN, additive guidance).

GAS does not always dominate GS: it underperforms GS at NFE>=5 on ImageNet and NFE>=6 on MS-COCO (Table 2), and its benefits are concentrated in the low-NFE regime, weakening the framing of adversarial training as a universally positive contribution.

Fairness of some baseline comparisons is questionable: several key S4S numbers are taken from other papers (with '†' caveats about different teacher hyperparameters) on LSUN and MS-COCO, and GS/GAS use the authors' own reimplementations of baselines elsewhere; teacher setups differ across rows (e.g., 'one-plus' teacher for SD), complicating direct comparison.

Scalability and applicability limits are acknowledged but unresolved: backpropagation through the entire multi-step solver chain is the bottleneck (so the method is unlikely to apply to the largest current models, which are precisely where sampling cost matters most), and a separate solver must be trained per NFE.
Method performs poorly at NFE=1-2 (FID 147+ on FFHQ, Table 11), so it does not address the extreme few-step regime where other acceleration approaches operate.

Minor presentation issues: the code URL in the abstract is missing, several passages contain grammatical errors ('perfomance', 'difference in teacher hyperparameters'), and the paper relies heavily on the appendix for details.
